utterances.text: During the conflict with NATO, General Geza Farkas was head of UB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was your immediate superior, he having been appointed --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- in place of Aleksandar Dimitrijevic, his predecessor.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Briefly about the flow of UB information at this time. Paragraph 200. Reporting put together for the Chief of the General Staff and other staff, and who had the ultimate decision of where reports went from Kosovo sources?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can talk about reports from the province of work of the security organs. They were sent along the vertical line up to the security administration, and selections were made at every lower level of command. As for this information, the Chief of General Staff was informed about all of them, and he decided which particular pieces of information would then be forwarded to the president of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that would be General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 201. Any crimes of which the UB became aware in the Pristina Corps would have been brought to the attention of General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And his obligation would be to have reported to whom?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have to report on the basis of selection as to what was relevant. He would have to report to the commander of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that would then take those reports, as appropriate, to General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the ultimate instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The general in charge of the 3rd Army at that stage being?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Nebojsa Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We saw on the bridge at Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The composition of the General Staff you've set out, and it would probably be easier if I simply read it. This was the General Staff during the state of war. Chief of General Staff, General Ojdanic. Deputy Chief of the General Staff, General Svetozar Marjanovic. Assistant to the Chief of the General Staff for operative affairs, General Blagoje Kovacevic. Assistant to the Chief of the General Staff for land forces, General Simic. Assistant to the Chief of the General Staff for the navy, Admiral Vlado Nokovic. Assistant to the General Staff for the air force, General Bane Petrovic. Head of the VJ Security Service, as we heard, General Geza Farkas. Assistant to the Chief of the General Staff for intelligence, General Branko Krga. Assistant to the Chief of the General Staff for logistics, General Pantelic. And at least until last week you did not remember the name of the assistant to the chief of the General Staff for morale.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 204. During the extraordinary states, as we've heard, the General Staff becomes known as the Supreme Command Staff, and the President of the FRY, as the Commander-in-Chief of the VJ, commands the VJ through the Supreme Command. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the term "Supreme Commander" gets used from time to time. To your knowledge, did it actually exist in the legislation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how things stand in -- on paper, but in fact, this is the Supreme Commander if the person concerned commands the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was that title appropriate for the accused?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Supreme Command comprised the Supreme Command Staff and what else or who else?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Supreme Defence Council. That's the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did this incorporate the Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: During the state of war, was the Supreme Command located in a single place or dispersed in various locations in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Various locations around Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there daily briefings of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know that. I know that the Supreme Command Staff met on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And representation of the UB on the General Staff or within the Supreme Command would come how?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security administration was not deployed at the same places where the Supreme Command Staff was, and usually one of the senior officers or a general would take part in the work of the Supreme Command Staff on a daily basis. But people took turns. It wasn't always the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can look at tab 37, please. There is a document purporting to be minutes of the 8th session of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 25th of December, 1998, in Belgrade. And have you reviewed it so as to be satisfied that it would seem to be generally representative of the materials that might be dealt with at such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present at such meetings. However, according to the form in line with which this document was made, I think that this does reflect the functioning of this type of body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see on the first page, and I'm not going to take you through very much of it, but we can see on the first page that the composition is the accused presiding, with the President of Serbia, Milan Milutinovic, and of Montenegro, Milo Djukanovic; together with vice-presidents of the federal government, Nikola Sainovic; Federal Minister of Defence, Pavle Bulatovic; and General Ojdanic as Chief of the General Staff; and Slavoljub Susic as Secretary of the Supreme Defence Council. That's the composition of this particular meeting. And if we go on to English page 13, and in the original unnumbered pages I think it will be about -- I'm afraid I can't find it for you. I think it may be about three or four pages in from the end. But there's a passage that begins with President Djukanovic not wanting to comment on candidates, especially because he personally knew only a couple of them, emphasising controversial information on the Pristina Corps engagement in Kosovo. Can you find that passage where, as the context of the document as a whole, you'll see that President Djukanovic --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we see in this paragraph President Djukanovic questioning Pavkovic's qualities. And then if we see the next paragraph down, we see the accused agreeing with Djukanovic's remarks that there were -- there's a mistake in the preparations and the lists were given together with the motions. After reviewing the documents, however, President Djukanovic said that the materials provided were sufficient. When commenting on his dilemma about General Pavkovic, the accused said there were no complaints from any side about unlawful behaviour of the Pristina Corps. This passage reflects what, so far as you're concerned -- and is it a topic of which you had knowledge contemporaneously?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about the general situation, the general debate that took place when General Pavkovic was supposed to be appointed. However, I'm not aware of these details, and therefore, I cannot give an assessment as to what was discussed and what the problems involved were, because it's written in rather general terms over here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was known publicly at the time -- or I say publicly. What was known to those of you in high office within the various parts of the forces and security services and so on? What was known about the appointment of Pavkovic and the attitudes taken by the accused and President Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what? President Djukanovic at that time was in a position of obstruction. Perhaps I can put it that way. Even vis-a-vis Yugoslavia as a whole. And I think that it is from that point of view that he put this question why these personnel proposed appointments were not submitted to him earlier. So his was a restrained position, a reserved position, and probably if he had something more specific on the situation in Kosovo and on the problems that he was speaking of, I assume that he would have said so. However, as for General Pavkovic, in that period of time it was widely known that the then-president of Yugoslavia was inclined towards him and that he definitely influenced his candidature and appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we turn to the accused's authority over the MUP. Was the MUP part of the -- formally part of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that with any certainty, but MUP was practically under the control of the accused along the vertical line that went through the Minister of the Interior of Serbia and then further on in-depth. However, at the time when I held these positions during the state of war, I am not aware that anyone from the MUP ever attended meetings of the Supreme Command Staff. That means that they did not attend meetings of the Supreme Command either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic again, as head of the RDB, what reporting was done by him to the accused?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to what degree, but he certainly had to report to him and inform him regularly, bearing in mind the fact that he was immediately subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you explain for the Chamber, please, the process whereby the accused's direction became an operational plan for the army of which he was effectively Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain that in principle. When the army or the chief of General Staff are issued a concrete order and when an objective is set that is to be achieved, then in principle in the staff the situation involved is assessed and proposals are presented on the way in which the armed forces could be used. This proposal as to the way in which the armed forces could be used should then be presented to the Supreme Commander by the chief of General Staff. And then upon his verification, this would come into effect, or certain corrections are made if any such corrections were made in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the authorisation of a proposal as amended, is this to be a signed document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, if this is a general directive on the use of the armed forces, there should be a signature, saying "I approve," and this means that this is approval of the Supreme Commander. This also refers to maps where the deployment of forces is actually charted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And once that step's been taken, is the next step to issue instructions to strategic groups of the decisions for the use of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so on down the chain of command from strategic groups to their various subordinate commands?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your summary, you make a reference to contingency plans existing even in peacetime. Perhaps obviously in a country surrounded by many other countries, there could have been contingency plans to cope with various possibilities; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would there be documents specifically approved and even signed by the accused, even if they needed fleshing out with detail should the relevant crisis occur?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know about the period when I did service at the JNA when states of emergency were proclaimed - twice actually - for the situation in Kosovo. But I don't know whether a state of emergency was proclaimed later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, then we won't trouble you with that earlier detail at this stage. Information going to the accused, please, from Ojdanic on what basis as to regularity?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I assume that he received daily reports which were compiled by the operations centre of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the Chief of the General Staff himself was kept informed by a regular reporting system upwards to him, with consolidation of information from lower units producing daily reports and other reports. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And might there be yet further reports informing Ojdanic outside Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of or certainly independent of the operations centre which would be handling the majority of regular reports?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be, because it was under his competence to command the strategic groups under him. So he could have received oral reports. He could have asked for special reports. So that is separate from the line going from the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll deal now with a meeting on the 1st of June, 1999, when you went to Kosovo to inspect the UB units. And while you were there, did General Pavkovic invite you to attend a meeting of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, but he didn't tell me that it was a meeting. He just told me to come to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you got there, did you find that it was indeed a meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting started soon afterwards. The meeting was chaired by Mr. Sainovic, and with him to attend the meeting Andjelkovic arrived, Zoran Andjelkovic. Of the generals, the JNA generals present, there was General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, myself, and colonel chief of security in the Pristina Corps with whom I came to the meeting. He was there too. From the MUP, there was General Djordjevic present, General Stevanovic, and General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you've mentioned Colonel Stojanovic. Was he significant and was he there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was chief of security of the Pristina Corps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was an absentee identified?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Djordjevic said that the absentee was General Ilic, that he wouldn't be attending the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the reason for his absence on this particular day, the 1st of June, 1999, was what?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what was said, he was on assignment with respect to cleaning up or mopping up the battleground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the particular word that we use for cleaning up or mopping up -- beg your pardon. The particular word that you use was what?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the prescribed procedure of doing away with the bodies, clearing the terrain of the bodies of people or animals and other noxious material that could have a negative effect on the health of the population, cause epidemics or other hazardous effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But is the word indeed "asanacija"?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "asanacija bojista."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The explanation for General Ilic's absence led you to conclude that he was a normal or regular attender?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any representative there from the state security, the RDB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You checked on the number of seats around the table and formed what view?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a seat that was empty, and that was the seat that probably should have been occupied by General Ilic. At the head of the table, in the presiding chair, was Mr. Sainovic, and to his left were Generals -- well, the colonel that I mentioned. To his right was Zoran Andjelkovic and the MUP generals. And opposite him, on the other side of the table to Mr. Sainovic, was General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this occasion where we have to deal with things normally fairly swiftly, I want you to help the Judges, please, with who had authority. Who was revealed as having authority, and how did that become clear? You said Sainovic was in the chair. How was he treated by all the others?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both according to his position around the table and also according to the other people's relationship and conduct towards him and by virtue of the fact that he in fact chaired the meeting, Mr. Sainovic had the dominant role in all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fact Mr. Nice, we have to adjourn on time today. We'll go on tomorrow. How much longer do you think you'll be with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should think at least the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. General Vasiljevic, will you be back, please, 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of February, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
